description: Infrastructure and deployments are defined as code / automated, not manual console changes.
evidence: Our CI/CD pipeline uses GitHub Actions to trigger Terraform, ensuring all AWS infrastructure is defined as code.

description: Monitoring, logging, and alerting are defined for the workload's key operational signals.
evidence: Datadog and AWS X-Ray provide our distributed tracing.

description: An incident response process or runbook is referenced for operational failures.
evidence: Standard SOPs and runbooks for general operational outages are still being drafted.

description: Changes can be rolled back safely; deployment approach limits blast radius of a bad change.
evidence: Deployments use AWS CodeDeploy for automated Blue/Green rollouts with safe rollback thresholds.

description: IAM roles/permissions follow least privilege rather than broad/wildcard access.
evidence: IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) restrict container permissions.

description: Sensitive or PII-bearing data stores have encryption at rest specified.
evidence: Data at rest (S3, DynamoDB, OpenSearch) uses KMS Customer Managed Keys.

description: Data in transit is encrypted (TLS) between components, especially over public networks.
evidence: Internal services use App Mesh for mTLS 1.3.

description: Credentials/API keys/secrets are managed via a secrets store, not hardcoded or embedded in config.
evidence: DevOps currently injects our Datadog APM and legacy CRM API keys as plaintext environment variables directly into the ECS task definitions.

description: Network boundaries/segmentation are defined; public-facing components are minimized and fronted appropriately.
evidence: AWS WAF and VPC Endpoints (PrivateLink) ensure no database or Bedrock traffic traverses the public internet.

description: Authentication/authorization (SSO, MFA, RBAC) is defined for user- and system-facing access.
evidence: End-users access the tool via AWS Cognito (OIDC federated to corporate Active Directory with MFA).

description: Security-relevant actions and access are logged in an auditable, tamper-resistant way.
evidence: CloudTrail is configured with log file validation to ensure tamper-resistant audit logs.

description: Critical components have redundancy (multi-AZ or equivalent) rather than a single point of failure.
evidence: Multi-AZ is enabled across ECS, OpenSearch, and NAT Gateways.

description: A disaster recovery approach with defined RTO/RPO is present for critical data/workloads.
evidence: We are targeting a 2-hour RTO and 15-minute RPO.

description: Dependent-service failures are isolated (retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, dead-letter queues) rather than cascading.
evidence: Synchronous calls to the downstream CRM lack circuit breakers or retry limits.

description: A backup strategy exists for stateful data with a defined restore process.
evidence: DynamoDB uses Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR).

description: Compute/storage choices match the actual workload pattern (e.g., serverless for spiky load) rather than over-provisioning.
evidence: Fargate auto-scales based on CPU utilization, easily accommodating our spiky intraday call volumes without over-provisioning.

description: Caching is used where repeated reads or expensive computations would otherwise recur.
evidence: Semantic caching via Amazon ElastiCache (Redis) catches repeated queries, skipping the Bedrock invocation entirely.

description: The database/storage type matches its access pattern (e.g., not using a relational store for pure key-value lookups at scale).
evidence: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless (chosen for its native K-NN similarity search performance).

description: Content/data delivery accounts for geographic distribution of users where relevant (CDN or regional deployment).
evidence: The frontend is a React SPA delivered via Amazon CloudFront (S3 origin).

description: Cost tracking/tagging/budgets are defined so spend is attributable and boundable.
evidence: No mention of cost tracking tags or budgets in the architecture document.

description: Resources scale down/to zero with demand rather than running at fixed capacity for variable load.
evidence: Fargate auto-scales based on CPU utilization

description: Storage has a lifecycle/retention policy rather than indefinite accumulation at full-cost tiers.
evidence: All ingested raw PDFs and session transcripts remain in the support-raw-logs S3 bucket indefinitely with no TTL or Glacier transition policy.

description: Provisioning model (on-demand vs reserved/provisioned) matches the workload's actual usage predictability.
evidence: Fargate auto-scales based on CPU utilization, easily accommodating our spiky intraday call volumes without over-provisioning.

description: Managed/serverless services are used where feasible to improve utilization over self-managed idle infrastructure.
evidence: Amazon API Gateway routes to our backend microservices, which run on AWS ECS Fargate

description: Data retention/storage footprint is minimized to what's needed rather than retained indefinitely by default.
evidence: All ingested raw PDFs and session transcripts remain in the support-raw-logs S3 bucket indefinitely with no TTL or Glacier transition policy.

description: Region/deployment choice shows awareness of energy/carbon considerations where it doesn't conflict with other constraints.
evidence: We have localized this deployment strictly to the eu-north-1 region to leverage its high renewable energy mix

description: AI-driven decisions that affect people can be explained at a level appropriate to the audience.
evidence: every response includes a strict citation linking back to the source PDF.

description: AI outputs are evaluated for unjustified variation across populations/segments where the use case involves consequential decisions.
evidence: No evaluations have been conducted to see if the bot's accuracy varies across different demographic segments of our user base.

description: LLM outputs are grounded (RAG, validation, citation) rather than relying on unverified generation for factual claims.
evidence: The RAG architecture heavily restricts the LLM to only use the retrieved OpenSearch context, controlling hallucinations

description: PII flowing through AI components is identified and protected (minimization, masking, or encryption).
evidence: A custom Python middleware and Amazon Macie scrub PII from user prompts before they reach Bedrock.

description: AI-specific threats (prompt injection, data poisoning, model extraction) are considered, not just traditional infra security.
evidence: Thorough red-teaming and threat modeling for prompt injection and data poisoning were completed last month.

description: An incident response path exists specifically for AI failures (bad output, hallucination, misuse), not just general system incidents.
evidence: there is no specialized response path for AI-specific failures (e.g., severe model drift or prompt jailbreaks).

description: AI models/outputs are validated (testing, red-teaming, or human review) before being relied upon in production.
evidence: Thorough red-teaming and threat modeling for prompt injection and data poisoning were completed last month.

description: Cost per AI call/decision is knowable or estimable, not opaque.
evidence: reduces our cost per query (which is logged granularly in DynamoDB)

description: Cheaper/smaller models are used for simple tasks, reserving expensive models for tasks that need them.
evidence: simple intent classification goes to Claude 3 Haiku, while complex summarization routes to Claude 3.5 Sonnet.

description: Repeated or semantically similar AI queries are cached rather than always re-invoking the model.
evidence: Semantic caching via Amazon ElastiCache (Redis) catches repeated queries, skipping the Bedrock invocation entirely.

description: Data residency/location constraints are explicit and enforced by design, not left implicit.
evidence: localized this deployment strictly to the eu-north-1 region to leverage its high renewable energy mix and enforce European data residency.

description: Foundation model/vendor dependency is acknowledged with some consideration of switching cost or exit path.
evidence: abstracts our Bedrock calls, meaning we can easily swap our provider to an open-source Llama model on SageMaker if vendor lock-in becomes an issue.

description: AI provider calls are abstracted behind an internal interface rather than tightly coupled to one vendor's SDK throughout the codebase.
evidence: the backend uses a custom FoundationModelGateway SDK. This abstracts our Bedrock calls

description: Consequential AI decisions retain a human review/override point rather than being fully autonomous.
evidence: The system operates autonomously, providing answers directly to the user interface without a human-in-the-loop review step for the generated text.

description: End users/operators have a defined path to understand and correctly use the AI system's outputs.
evidence: They must complete a mandatory Wiki training module on AI limitations before being granted IAM access.

description: Design choices (model size, caching, batching) that reduce cost also incidentally reduce AI inference energy footprint.
evidence: simple intent classification goes to Claude 3 Haiku... This reduces our cost per query... and lowers our inference energy footprint.

description: Each AI model/component in the design has a clear named owner and purpose.
evidence: Jane Doe (VP of Data Science) is the named owner of this model

description: AI decisions/outputs are logged with enough context (input, model version, output) to be reconstructed later.
evidence: No mention of logging AI prompts, contexts, and outputs for reconstruction.

description: It's clear who is accountable when the AI produces an incorrect or harmful output.
evidence: Jane Doe (VP of Data Science) is the named owner of this model and holds ultimate accountability for its outputs.
